newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - DEC 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - DEC 5.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:
KATHIMERINI

--Northern Greece is facing the loss of its comparitive edge in the Balkan and central and eastern European markets as all economic activity grinds to a halt in the face of the continuing road blockade and port strike. Customers from abroad have begun cancelling orders as the farmers' protest enters its eighth day.

--Greece's telecommunications organisation OTE has begun its search for a managing consultant with a first candidate being rejected. The search has moved to leading executives of Greek descent from America.

--The Capital Market Commission has asked for new clarifications of the sale or movement of shares without the knowledge of bourse authorities from major stock holders in 40 listed companies. Sources say the question of how to deal with violations will be dealt with in the new year.
IMERISIA

--National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou yesterday submitted the government's tax bill to Parliament. Wage-earners will pay more for the so-called "convergence taxes" due to the non-indexation of income brackets. Fines of up to 150 percent of the tax are foreseen for those making inaccurate or misleading real estate tax declarations.
--Some 135.9 billion drachmas will be allocated from the Publicv Investment Programme for road works in 1997, while the Athens Metro and natural gas projects will also get a sizeable share.

--The government is considering a round of taxes on state titles for 1998 and beyond which will increase the rate from 7.5 percent to 15.0 percent. Deputy Finance Minister Nikos Christodoulakis said the government was working on a law which would make it impossible for investors to avoid paying the tax.
--National Bank of Greece Governor Theodoros Karatzas predicted yesterday that the next few years will see the local banking market transformed.
KERDOS

--The meeting between Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas and protesting farmers in Larissa yesterday was a complete failure as both sides stuck to their guns. The impasse forced businessmen in Northern Greece to send a message to the prime minister telling him that many were facing major problems and some would not be able to pay Christmas bonuses to workers.

--If the road blocks by the farmers continue, the forecast target of below 8.0 percent inflation for the end of the year will not be met, despite an expected drop in the consumer price index to 7.9 percent in November, compared to 8.3 percent in October.
--The rise in the dollar has caused a small increase in retil fuel prices.
EXPRESS
--Today will also see a decision on whether port employees strike indefinitely. Sources say however there will be a solution to their problems by the end of the year.
--The issue of how the tax on derivatives and financial products is to be levied has been left out of the new taxation bill.
NAFTEMBORIKI
--Industry and exporters in major towns and cities cry for help as they bear the brunt of the continuing blockade on the roads and ports.
--Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
